rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects literal severing: bone-cutting would require force and cutting at a joint deliberate care; the women likely scored their hands with what they held.
rows.anchor: والقطع على المفصل لا يتهيأ إلا بتلطف لا بد أن يقصد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled tāʾ in qaṭṭaʿna reflects the many women and repeated cuts, perhaps several cuts each.
rows.anchor: وضوعفت الطاء في قطعن لكثرتهن وكثرة الحز فربما كان مرارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ubayy, and Ibn Masʿūd read ḥāshā Allāh; the other seven read ḥāsh li-llāh; a group has ḥashā; al-Ḥasan has a weak vowelless-shīn form and also ḥāsh al-ilāh.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وحده «حاشى الله»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh treats ḥāsh as an exception particle governing genitive, while al-Mubarrad favors the verbal use with accusative because ḥāsh li-Zayd shows it is a verb.
rows.anchor: فأما «حاش» فهي حيث جرت حرف معناه الاستثناء، كذا قال سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya synthesizes them: the particle governs genitive and the verb accusative; the verb means removing someone from an associated attribution, like the imagery of ḥashā and ḥāshiya.
rows.anchor: يظهر من مجموع كلام سيبويه والمبرد أن الحرف يخفض به لا غير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ḥāshā is verbal because it is followed by a preposition, which a preposition cannot follow; deletion of its yāʾ in another reading supports this.
rows.anchor: ومن المواضع التي حاشى فيه فعل هذه الآية، يدل على ذلك دخولها على حرف الجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deletion without a doubled consonant is unusual, though mundhu is an exception to the stated condition.
rows.anchor: بمنذ وفد حذف دون تضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report about Khālid on the day of Muʾta uses fa-ḥāshā bi-l-nās, illustrating the verb's sense of moving people aside.
rows.anchor: في حديث خالد يوم مؤتة: فحاشى بالناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī explains ḥāshā li-llāh as exempting or protecting Joseph for God's obedience, favor, or elevation, and denying that he is a god because such conduct belongs to humans.
rows.anchor: هكذا رتب أبو علي- الفارسي معنى هذا الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd's reading can instead be an exception particle, as in Ibn ʿAṭiyya's poem exempting Abū Thawbān from blame and insult.
rows.anchor: حاشى أبي ثوبان إن به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan's vowelless-shīn reading is weak because it brings two vowelless consonants together; his other reading drops the alif of ḥāshā.
rows.anchor: وتسكين الشين في إحدى قراءتي الحسن، ضعيف، جمع بين ساكنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Joseph an angel is an exalted comparison to an unseen, venerated being.
rows.anchor: والتشبيه بالملك هو من قبيل التشبيه بالمستعظمات وإن كانت لا ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥuwayrith al-Ḥanafī and al-Ḥasan read malik, ‘king’; on that reading the women distinguish a purchasable human slave from a noble king.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو الحويرث الحنفي والحسن «ما هذا بشر إن هذا إلا ملك كريم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative basharan follows the Hijaz dialect, which treats mā like laysa; Tamīm uses the nominative, though that form was not read.
rows.anchor: هو على لغة الحجاز شبهت ما بليس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports assign Joseph a third or half of beauty; the half-beauty report differs over whether his mother or Sarah, his paternal grandmother, shared it.
rows.anchor: وروي أن يوسف عليه السلام أعطي ثلث الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes the beauty fractions figuratively: they make the listener feel Joseph's extraordinary beauty, like comparisons with devils' heads and ogres' teeth.
rows.anchor: وهذا على جهة التمثيل، أي لو كان الحسن مما يقسم

rows.speaker: السدي وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and Ibn Isḥāq say Joseph shifted the prisoners away from interpreting their bread dream, which signaled a death, by promising to explain food dreams before their outcomes appeared.
rows.anchor: روي عن السدي وابن إسحاق: أن يوسف عليه السلام لما علم شدة تعبير منامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prisoners challenged Joseph's source of knowledge; he credited his Lord, then preached against disbelief both to divert them from a fatal interpretation and to win faith for their afterlife.
rows.anchor: ثم نهض ينحي لهما على الكفر ويحسن لهما الإيمان بالله

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj reads Joseph's promise as foretelling the outcome of waking food before it arrives, implying knowledge of unseen matters unrelated to dreams; the author links this to prophethood in prison.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: أراد يوسف عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj also says the king sent food to prisoners he intended to execute as a sign of their death.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: كانت عادة ذلك الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says these prison-food explanations are neither required by the wording nor supported by a sound chain.
rows.anchor: لا يقتضيه اللفظ ولا ينهض به إسناد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph can say he ‘left’ a religion he never embraced because he avoided it from the outset; speaking of leaving it may draw the prisoners toward abandoning it too.
rows.anchor: وقوله: تركت مع أنه لم يتشبث بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people whose religion Joseph left are the king and his followers; repeating ‘they’ emphasizes the point and suits the verse's cadence.
rows.anchor: والقوم المتروكة ملتهم: الملك وأتباعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph continues inviting the prisoners to the upright faith of his forefathers while avoiding direct confrontation with the import of their dreams.
rows.anchor: تماد من يوسف عليه السلام في دعائهما إلى الملة الحنيفية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī and Abū ʿAmr read ābāya with a still yāʾ; most readers open it. Abū Ḥātim accepts both; dropping the hamza is invalid, while easing it is sound.
rows.anchor: وقرأ «آبائي» بالإسكان في الياء الأشهب العقيلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘That’ points to the forefathers' religion and law: choosing them as prophets favors them, while their call saves people from God's punishment.
rows.anchor: وقوله: ذلك إشارة إلى ملتهم وشرعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The min in mā kāna lanā min shayʾ is emphatic after negation; ‘most people do not give thanks’ means they lack complete gratitude, which includes faith.
rows.anchor: من شيء هي من الزائدة المؤكدة التي تكون مع الجحد

rows.speaker: جماعة من أهل التأويل
rows.claim: A group of exegetes assigns the statement to Joseph: he wants his master to know he did not betray his family while absent, and that God does not bring a traitor's plot to success.
rows.anchor: قالت جماعة من أهل التأويل: هذه المقالة هي من يوسف عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Guiding’ a plot is metaphorical: God does not perfect or carry it along a successful path, though a righteous person's beneficial plot may be guided.
rows.anchor: والهدى للكيد مستعار، بمعنى لا يكلمه ولا يمضيه على طريق إصابة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj connects Joseph's words to 12:50 and says the discourse uses fronting and delay; ‘that’ means remaining in prison while seeking vindication.
rows.anchor: فالإشارة بقوله: ذلك- على هذا التأويل- هي إلى بقائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view has Joseph speak after the wife's confession in 12:51, with ‘that’ referring to her admission and God's favor; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects it because Joseph would be present before the later summons in 12:54.
rows.anchor: وهذا يضعف، لأنه يقتضي حضوره مع النسوة

rows.speaker: فرقة من أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Another group assigns the continuous statement to the wife: her confession lets Joseph know she did not lie about or falsely accuse him in his absence; the implied subject is her repentance and admission.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة من أهل التأويل: هذه الآية من قول امرأة العزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether ‘I do not absolve myself’ belongs to Joseph or the wife follows the disputed attribution of the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: هذه أيضا مختلف فيها هل هي من كلام يوسف أم من كلام المرأة

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: A report from Anas traces to the Prophet: Gabriel rebuked Joseph's claim of not betraying in secret by recalling his earlier desire; Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrima, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk reportedly give a similar account.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī reports that the woman said the self-reproach, while another report from Ibn ʿAbbās says Joseph remembered his prior desire and said it himself.
rows.anchor: قاله السدي، وروي أن يوسف تذكر من تلقائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the wife speaks, she excuses her desire as an ordinary human failing: human souls strongly urge evil and no one can claim exemption.
rows.anchor: ومن قال: إن المرأة قالت وما أبرئ نفسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ammāra is an intensive form. Most grammarians take mā in illā mā raḥima as a verbal noun, yielding a disconnected exception for God's mercy.
rows.anchor: وأمارة بناء مبالغة، وما في قوله: إلا ما رحم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī allows mā to mean man, ‘except the souls God has mercy on,’ since nafs can be collective for rational beings; Ibn ʿAṭiyya accepts mā for a noun-class.
rows.anchor: كذا قال أبو علي، فتقدير الآية: إلا النفوس التي يرحمها الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the collective noun use validates mā for people, citing al-Mubarrad and reading this as Sībawayhi's and Abū ʿAlī's position.
rows.anchor: وهو نص في كلام المبرد، وهو- عندي- معنى كلام سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā may instead be temporal: the self urges evil except during the period when God has mercy on a person and he abandons sinful desire.
rows.anchor: أن النفس لأمارة بالسوء إلا مدة رحمة الله العبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse ends by hoping in God's forgiveness and mercy.
rows.anchor: ثم ترجى في آخر الآية بقوله: إن ربي غفور رحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once the king recognized Joseph's innocence, trustworthiness, patience, and endurance, Joseph's standing rose and the king asked to keep him close.
rows.anchor: لما تبينت له براءة يوسف مما نسب إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The progression from a bare summons at 12:50 to a close-adviser appointment shows Joseph's trustworthiness, patience, high purpose, good judgment, and eloquence confirmed or surpassed what was reported.
rows.anchor: فلما فعل يوسف ما فعل، فظهرت أمانته وصبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makīn means established in rank; amīn means trustworthy, though some say it means secure.
rows.anchor: وأمين من الأمانة، وقالت فرقة هو بمعنى آمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects ‘secure’ as a weak sense of amīn because it disrupts the parallel and diminishes Joseph's honor.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف، لأنه يخرج من نمط الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the king offered to share everything except his family and meals; Joseph answered that, as Abraham's, Isaac's, and Jacob's descendant, he had more reason to refuse.
rows.anchor: إني أشاركك في كل شيء إلا أني أحب أن لا تشركني في أهلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the king-and-meal story weak; Ibn Maysara instead places it earlier, when Joseph ate with the Aziz and the wife objected.
rows.anchor: وقد قال ابن ميسرة: إنما جرى هذا في أول أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent account still has Joseph enslaved while speaking with the king; otherwise he would distance himself from service to idolaters, as his prison conversations show.
rows.anchor: الظاهر من قصته وقت محاورة الملك أنه كان على عبودية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God calls Egypt's ruler ‘king’ retrospectively; using king or emir for a living unbeliever would recognize his rule, so the Prophet addressed Heraclius as ‘great of the Romans.’
rows.anchor: وسمى الله تعالى فرعون مصر ملكا إذ هي حكاية اسم مضى حكمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The descriptive title ‘great’ remains true in every state, unlike a ruling title; calling Heraclius emir could furnish him an argument, as in Ziyād's appeal to ʿAlī's testimony.
rows.anchor: وأما كونه عظيمهم فتلك صفة لا تفارقه كيفما تقلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph understood that the king meant to entrust him with administration, so he sought the office where he could establish justice, benefit rightful recipients, and put things in proper hands.
rows.anchor: فألقى يده في الفصل الذي تمكنه فيه المعدلة

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some exegetes say a virtuous person may work for a wicked ruler if entrusted with a field where he can act justly; service governed by arbitrary desires and wrongdoing is forbidden.
rows.anchor: قال بعض أهل التأويل: في هذه الآية ما يبيح للرجل الفاضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph sought office as religious service to establish justice; like Abū Bakr accepting the caliphate, a virtuous person may seek work when no substitute can do it and truthfully praise himself if his merit is unknown.
rows.anchor: وطلبة يوسف للعمل إنما هي حسبة منه عليه السلام لرغبته في أن يقع العدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khazāʾin is a general term for everything stored by the kingdom, including food and wealth.
rows.anchor: وخزائن لفظ عام لجميع ما تختزنه المملكة من طعام ومال وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥafīẓ and ʿalīm are broad qualifications: Joseph can protect all aspects of the stores and understand all matters of administration; narrower readings are unwarranted.
rows.anchor: وحفيظ عليم صفتان تعم وجوه التثقيف والحيطة لا خلل معهما لعامل

rows.speaker: مالك بن أنس
rows.claim: Mālik ibn Anas calls Egypt the storehouse of the earth and adduces this verse as evidence.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مالك بن أنس أنه قال: مصر خزانة الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘storehouses of the earth’ are Egypt, Pharaoh's only kingdom; its central location made it a hub from which goods moved to the world's regions.
rows.anchor: وقوله خزائن الأرض يريد أرض مصر إذ لم تكن مملكة فرعون إلا بها فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Thus We established Joseph’ points back to God's gracious acts: He advanced Joseph through ranks until he had secure standing in the land.
rows.anchor: الإشارة بذلك إلى ما تقدم من جميل صنع الله به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports disagree whether the Aziz died soon or was dismissed and later died; Ibn Isḥāq adds Joseph's appointment and marriage to his wife, who said she had been a virgin and bore two sons.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: بل عزله الملك ثم مات أطفير

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: A long report says Joseph eventually dominated the kingdom and the king accepted Islam; the former Aziz died poor, while his aged, lame wife met Joseph, praised God's reversal of fortune, and was restored to beauty and married him.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: وأسلم الملك آخر أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya warns that many surrounding stories cannot be authenticated and would make the discussion needlessly long.
rows.anchor: وروي في نحو هذا من القصص ما لا يوقف على صحته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read ‘where he wills’ of Joseph; Ibn Kathīr alone reads ‘where We will,’ also reported by Abū Ḥātim from other Medinese readers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: «حيث يشاء» على الإخبار عن يوسف

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī explains the first-person reading either as places of worship God wills, or Joseph's will attributed to God because his servant's will operates by God's power, comparing 8:17.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: إما أن يكون تقدير هذه القراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls Abū ʿAlī's explanation a Muʿtazilī inclination that avoids saying human actions have two agents.
rows.anchor: وهذا كله من أبي على نزغة اعتزالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in makannā li-Yūsuf is compared with 27:72 and 12:43; yatabawwaʾu is a circumstantial accusative, and ḥaythu is an adverb or object, as al-Shammākh's verse shows.
rows.anchor: وقوله: يتبوأ في موضع نصب على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse turns from Joseph's rewarded worldly virtue to the better afterlife as the proper aim for believers and the God-fearing, and hints his hereafter exceeds his worldly rank.
rows.anchor: عقب ذلك بأن حال الآخرة أحمد وأحرى أن تجعل غرضا ومقصدا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and others say famine struck Jacob's region, located variously in Palestinian lowlands or nearby; Egypt had stored surplus and Joseph rationed each visitor one camel-load equally.
rows.anchor: قال السدي وغيره: سبب مجيئهم أن الجماعة التي أنذر بها يوسف أصابت البلاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph recognized his brothers, while they failed to recognize him because of long separation and changed age; his royal status and Coptic speech kept them from suspecting him.
rows.anchor: فلما ورد إخوته عرفهم يوسف ولم يعرفوه هم، لبعد العهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In story reports Joseph called them spies through an interpreter; they explained their family and missing brother, so he demanded Benjamin to verify their account and their father's preference.
rows.anchor: أظنكم جواسيس، فاحتاجوا- حينئذ- إلى التعريف بأنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other tales describe their formal audience, Joseph veiled, testing truth by the vessel's tone, and requiring the youngest; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the Qur'an only alludes briefly to this long story.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه كان متلثما أبدا سترا لجماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jihāz means a traveler's provisions, belongings, and carried goods; it also names a bride's or deceased person's outfit.
rows.anchor: ما يحتاج إليه المسافر من زاد ومتاع وكل ما يحمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's assurance about full measure and good hospitality reassures the brothers; munzilīn means hosts in his land and time, and the supplies are the food loaded for them.
rows.anchor: المنزلين يعني المضيفين في قطره ووقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph threatens to withhold future grain and bars them from approaching; lā taqrabūn may be a direct prohibition or an indicative form carrying prohibition, with one nūn elided.
rows.anchor: ولا تقربون نهي لفظا ومعنى

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik infers that grain measurement falls on the seller; agency and partnership resemble sale, while the borrower measures grain in a loan.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك رحمه الله: هذه الآية وما يليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports differ whether Joseph detained Simeon. A Prophetic report says a pebble dropped into the king's bowl rang and revealed their father; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it a possible trick.
rows.anchor: وروي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports say the bowl measured grain during scarcity and Joseph acquired people's property and land in the famine; the author says his actions were by revelation to complete Jacob's trial and first dream.
rows.anchor: وروي: أن ذلك الإناء به كان يكيل الطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers mean they will persistently negotiate with their father to let Benjamin go; they reinforce the promise by saying they will certainly do it.
rows.anchor: أي سنفائل أباه في أن يتركه يأتي معنا إليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph puts each brother's payment back among his provisions to draw them back through generosity and recognition of his favor.
rows.anchor: رد مال كل واحد منهم في رحله بين طعامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read fityatī; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read fityānī, with an uncertain ʿĀṣim reading. The plurals reflect fewer recipients or more servants and apply to free or enslaved men.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر: «لفتيته»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Perhaps they will recognize it’ means recognize Joseph's favor and return; the author rejects the view that he returned payment to force them to pay, since their delight shows his purpose was generosity.
rows.anchor: وإنما قصد أن يستميلهم ويصلهم، فيرغبهم في نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He returned their familiar, lawful payment rather than his less familiar wealth; other views say Jacob lacked cash or the returned goods foreshadow the cup and Benjamin's innocence.
rows.anchor: لأنها أوقع في نفوسهم، إذ يعرفون حلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's support of impoverished relatives was apparently obligatory because he was a just ruler and they were people of faith and prophethood.
rows.anchor: ما فعل يوسف من صلتهم، وجبرهم في تلك الشدة كان واجبا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers say naktal, echoing ‘measure is withheld from us’; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read yaktal, meaning Benjamin will measure for them as they had measured.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر: «نكتل»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naktal follows the iftiʿāl pattern; ‘measure was withheld’ most likely fears Joseph's future refusal after his threat, not Benjamin's missing camel-load.
rows.anchor: فهو خوف في المستأنف وقيل: أشاروا إلى بعير بنيامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers promise to protect Benjamin.
rows.anchor: ثم تضمنوا له حفظه وحيطته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's question is a rebuke and reminder that they proved unreliable; he does not forbid Benjamin's trip because he sees benefit, but reveals his anxiety and entrusts matters to God.
rows.anchor: قوله هل توقيف وتقرير، وتألم يعقوب عليه السلام من فرقة بنيامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers seem to have become prophets, so Jacob fears less than when Joseph disappeared, though his words still differ from his earlier expression.
rows.anchor: لكن ظاهر أمرهم أنهم كانوا نبئوا وانتقلت حالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read khayrun ḥifẓan; Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ read ḥāfiẓan. Both are accusative specifications; al-Zajjāj permits a circumstantial accusative, which Abū ʿAlī rejects as essential to the sense.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم- في رواية أبي بكر- «خير حفظا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading ḥifẓan echoes ‘we will protect him,’ while ḥāfiẓan echoes ‘we are his protectors’; both affirm that God's protection is best.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ «حفظا» فهو مع قولهم: ونحفظ أخانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd's reading ‘God is the best protector and He is the best of guardians’ is remote.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن مسعود: «فالله خير حافظ وهو خير الحافظين»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tied and packed load is called matāʿ, explaining the wording ‘they opened their belongings.’
rows.anchor: سمى المشدود المربوط بحملته متاعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read rudd at with ḍamma, followed by imāla and then kasra; ʿAlqama and Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb use kasra in Banū Ḍabba's dialect, analogized to qīla and bīʿa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علقمة ويحيى بن وثاب «ردت» بكسر الراء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes mā nabghī as a question from seeking: what more could they want after the returned payment and provisions?
rows.anchor: ما استفهاما، قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj also reads mā as a negation: nothing remains for them to seek; alternatively, from transgression, they deny wrongdoing or lying about the king's generosity.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: ويحتمل أن تكون ما نافية

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥaywa reads tabghī in the second person to Jacob, ‘what do you seek?’; al-Mahdawī says ʿĀʾisha transmitted this from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: على مخاطبة يعقوب، وهي بمعنى: ما تريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read numīru with fatḥa, from māra yamīru, ‘bring provisions,’ as in a poem; ʿĀʾisha and al-Sulamī read it with ḍamma, from a form synonymous with māra.
rows.anchor: من مار يمير: إذا جلب الخير

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The extra camel-load is Benjamin's, since Joseph gave the ten brothers provisions but no eleventh load; Mujāhid instead says ‘donkey-load,’ because some Arabs call a donkey baʿīr, which the author calls rare.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: كيل بعير أراد كيل حمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhālika kaylun yasīr may challenge whether a small measure can be neglected in famine, or mean it is easy for Joseph to grant; al-Ḥasan says he promised an extra free load, and al-Suddī says it would be quick.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن البصري: وقد كان يوسف وعدهم أن يزيدهم حمل بعير بغير ثمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Suddī's reading the brothers reassure Jacob that the extra measure will be quick and will not delay their return.
rows.anchor: فكأنهم أنسوه على هذا بقرب الأوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob asks for a firm pledge, from the root of strength; by naming God their guarantor he makes Him witness, protector, and surety of their agreement.
rows.anchor: أراد يعقوب عليه السلام أن يتوثق منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr retains the yāʾ in tuʾtūnī in pause and connection; Nāfiʿ reportedly retains it only in connection, while other readers omit it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير «تؤتوني» بياء في الوصل والوقف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatāda, and others say Jacob feared the evil eye because his eleven handsome, strong sons might draw envy; they affirm it and cite Prophetic warnings and a protective prayer.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والضحاك وقتادة وغيره: والعين حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation is that the brothers might look like spies, recalling Joseph's accusation; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak because they had already openly appeared in Egypt.
rows.anchor: ويضعف هذا ظهورهم قبل بمصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idea that Jacob hoped a split group would investigate Joseph is weak, since it does not fit his statement that he cannot protect them from God.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف يرده: وما أغني عنكم من الله من شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Unless you are surrounded’ broadly means total defeat or coercion leaving no escape; Mujāhid says all die, while Qatāda says they cannot comply, which better fits the wording.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: المعنى: إلا أن تهلكوا جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob combines a pledge, counsel, and precautions with reliance on God; believers' trust normally includes lawful means, not total abandonment of effort.
rows.anchor: فهذا توكل مع تسبب، وهو توكل جميع المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Law-giving prophets affirm legitimate means; casting oneself into danger is disputed, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects those who prefer it.
rows.anchor: والشارعون منهم مثبتون سنن التسبب الجائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Jacob asked the brothers to greet Egypt's king and say their father prays for him and thanks him; Abū Manṣūr al-Mahrānī says Joseph wept when the letter was read.
rows.anchor: قال لهم: بلغوا ملك مصر سلامي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Except a need in Jacob's soul’ means their precautions could not avert God's decree but fulfilled and soothed Jacob's desire; the exception is separate from the preceding clause.
rows.anchor: لم يكن في ذلك دفع قدر الله بل كان أربا ليعقوب قضاه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Ibn Isḥāq identify Jacob's need as fear of the evil eye; the author calls their wording figurative and cites a Prophetic report about blocking a grave opening to comfort the living.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: «الحاجة» : خيفة العين، وقاله ابن إسحاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The precaution could not repel a decree: an eye destined to strike would do so whether the brothers were together or apart; Jacob hoped his counsel might coincide with safety.
rows.anchor: لو قضي أن تصيبهم عين لأصابتهم مفترقين أو مجتمعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God praises Jacob as having insight taught by God, while most people do not know it.
rows.anchor: ثم أثنى الله عز وجل على يعقوب بأنه لقن ما علمه الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets Jacob's knowledge as acting on what God taught; Sufyān says one who does not act is not truly knowledgeable. The author says this exceeds the wording, though it is sound in itself.
rows.anchor: قاله قتادة- وقال سفيان: من لا يعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥātim records al-Aʿmash reading la-dhū ʿilmin limā ʿallamnāh; an answer to lammā may also be omitted.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حاتم: قرأ الأعمش لذو علم لما علمناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph welcomed Benjamin, his full brother, and āwā shares its root with al-maʾwā, a refuge.
rows.anchor: ومن هذه الكلمة المأوى

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq and others say the brothers were lodged in pairs, leaving Benjamin alone; Joseph roomed with him, disclosed his identity, and told him not to grieve over the plan against the others.
rows.anchor: على ما روي عن ابن إسحاق وغيره- أن يوسف عليه السلام أمر صاحب ضيافته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What they used to do’ may refer to Joseph's servants carrying out the cup plan or to the brothers' earlier wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: إلى ما يعمله فتيان يوسف

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih says Joseph called Benjamin brother only in affection, did not reveal his identity, and left him subject to the same stratagem as the others.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه: إنما أخبره أنه أخوه في الود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabtaʾis is a reflexive form of buʾs, meaning not to grieve or be distressed, as commentators explain.
rows.anchor: أي لا تحزن ولا تهتم، وهكذا عبر المفسرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says God revealed the full scheme: Jacob's law enslaved a thief, unlike Egypt's flogging and doubled restitution, so Joseph relied on his brothers invoking their rule despite the distress; al-Ṭabarī prefers the view that revelation only directed him to place the cup.
rows.anchor: في دين يعقوب أن يستعبد السارق، وكان في دين مصر أن يضرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Joseph deemed the accusation permissible because the brothers had sold him, and they were punished when they later said his brother had stolen.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم لما كانوا قد باعوا يوسف استجاز أن يقال لهم هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘He placed’ means Joseph ordered his servants and attendants to put the vessel in Benjamin's pack.
rows.anchor: وقوله: جعل أي بأمره خدمته وفتيانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads an extra wāw; most commentators identify the siqāya as the king's drinking cup and grain measure.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود «وجعل» بزيادة واو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some describe the vessel as double-ended with a central handle, measuring grain at one end and serving royal guests at the other; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr compares it to a tall Persian cup and cites Ibn ʿAbbās on al-ʿAbbās's similar cup.
rows.anchor: أنها شكل له رأسان ويصل بينهما مقبض

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr also calls the ṣuwāʿ a Persian-style open-ended drinking cup; reports variously make it silver, gold, musk-like, cup-shaped, or copper.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير- أيضا- «الصواع» : المكوك الفارسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because food was scarce, measuring was restricted to this special vessel; al-Suddī says Benjamin did not know it had been planted, which the author finds apparent.
rows.anchor: ولعزة الطعام في تلك الأعوام قصر كيلها على ذلك الإناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports differ whether the caravan was detained after leaving Egypt or before exiting; addressing the caravan is figurative for addressing its owners or party.
rows.anchor: فلما فصلت العير بأوفارها وخرجت من مصر- فيما روي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the brothers' animals were donkeys; the whole caravan is called thieves because one member appeared to steal, as when a tribe is said to kill though one man did it.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: كانت دوابهم حميرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers ask what is missing so a search can establish their innocence; they do not immediately deny the charge, hoping details might disprove it without a quarrel.
rows.anchor: بل سألوا إكمال الدعوى عسى أن يكون فيها ما تبطل به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān reads tufqidūn with ḍamma on tāʾ, which Abū Ḥātim considers weak.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عبد الرحمن: «تفقدون» بضم التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king's ṣuwāʿ is the measuring cup, that is, the siqāya, used from either of its two sides.
rows.anchor: وهو المكيال وهو السقاية رسمه أولا بإحدى جهتيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary among ṣuwāʿ, ṣāʿ, ṣūʿ, ṣūgh, and ṣuwāgh; these measure or vessel names may be masculine or feminine, depending on whether the word means a measure or cup.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس «صواع» بضم الصاد وبألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel-load reward is for identifying the thief and recovering the cup; the announcer personally guarantees it because he fears a promise made on the king's behalf will not be trusted.
rows.anchor: لمن دل على سارقه وفضحه وجبر الصواع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the guarantor as announcer; zaʿīm means guarantor and also leader because a leader takes responsibility for people's needs.
rows.anchor: «الزعيم» : الضامن- في كلام العرب- ويسمى الرئيس زعيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath ta-llāh substitutes tāʾ for wāw; tāʾ in an oath is restricted to the written divine name Allāh, not al-Raḥmān or al-Raḥīm.
rows.anchor: والتاء في تالله بدل من واو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports say the brothers cited returning money and avoiding unpaid food, or their reputation for piety and stopping camels from eating others' crops, to establish they were not thieves.
rows.anchor: روي: أن إخوة يوسف كانوا ردوا البضاعة الموجودة في الرحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servants ask the punishment if the brothers' denial is false; their answer means whoever has the cup in his pack becomes the punishment, with alternative grammatical parses for jazāʾahu.
rows.anchor: فقال إخوة يوسف: جزاء السارق والحكم الذي تتضمنه هذه الألفاظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' pledge exceeds their law: they agree to take anyone found with the cup as a thief, though only proven theft warranted seizure; their rule makes a thief's property the victim's.
rows.anchor: وهذا أكثر من موجب شرعهم إذ حق شرعهم أن لا يؤخذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the claim that this penalty existed in early Islam and was later abrogated by amputation, saying he knows of no such rule.
rows.anchor: أن هذا الحكم كان في أول الإسلام ثم نسخ بالقطع، وهذا ضعيف

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Zahrāwī transmits from al-Suddī that their law put a thief to work according to the value stolen; the author objects that the cup was returned, leaving nothing for Benjamin to work off.
rows.anchor: وحكى الزهراوي عن السدي: أن حكمهم إنما كان أن يستخدم السارق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Searching the other brothers' bags before Benjamin's makes Joseph's plan more convincing and hides the appearance of a trick.
rows.anchor: بدؤه- أيضا- من أوعيتهم تمكين للحيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read wiʿāʾ with kasra, al-Ḥasan with ḍamma, and Ibn Jubayr with hamza replacing wāw, a common shift with kasra and even more common with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس «وعاء» بكسر الواو

rows.speaker: السدي والضحاك
rows.claim: God's attribution of the stratagem describes enabling Joseph to take his brother; al-Suddī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk gloss kadnā as ‘We made/planned.’
rows.anchor: وقال السدي والضحاك: كدنا معناه: صنعنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the king's dīn as his sovereignty, and Qatāda as his rule or judgment; the author considers these close meanings.
rows.anchor: ودين الملك فسره ابن عباس بسلطانه، وفسره قتادة بالقضاء والحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception ‘unless God wills’ recounts the actual situation: God willed this stratagem; alternatively an implicit decree may be supplied to sustain the negation.
rows.anchor: والاستثناء في هذه الآية حكاية حال، التقدير: إلا أن شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read narfaʿ and nashāʾ in first-person plural; al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and Yaʿqūb use third-person singular. Readers also differ over annexation or tanwīn of darajāt.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «نرفع» على ضمير المعظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read ‘above every possessor of knowledge’; Ibn Masʿūd reads ‘above every knowledgeable person,’ parsed with an extra dhū or with ʿālim as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور، «وفوق كل ذي علم»

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda, also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, take the saying to mean people of knowledge have degrees and each scholar has someone more learned, human or God.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أن البشر في العلم درجات، فكل عالم فلا بد من أعلم منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the searcher repented and asked God's forgiveness after each bag search that found nothing.
rows.anchor: وروي أن المفتش كان إذا فرغ من رحل رجل فلم يجد فيه شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qatāda and others identify the searcher as Joseph, who knew the cup's location; this apparent self-directed action was still under God's command, as ‘We schemed’ confirms, since he needed their law to take Benjamin.
rows.anchor: وظاهر كلام قتادة وغيره، أن المستغفر كان يوسف لأنه كان يفتشهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘then he extracted it’ may refer to the vessel from 12:70 or to the theft itself.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله: استخرجها عائد على السقاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the brothers blamed Benjamin as the son of a mother who bore two thieves; he denied the theft and answered that whoever planted the cup also put their money in their bags.
rows.anchor: وروي أن إخوة يوسف لما رأوا ذلك قالوا: يا بنيامين بن راحيل

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda, also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, read the saying as a hierarchy among human scholars.
rows.anchor: هو قول الحسن وقتادة، وقد روي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās says only God is the Knower above every knower; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes this differs from al-Ḥasan's view.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: بئس ما قلت، إنما العليم لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' ‘his brother’ means Joseph, whom they leave unnamed to belittle him and attach the accusation to Benjamin as his full brother.
rows.anchor: والأخ الذي أشاروا إليه هو يوسف، ونكروه تحقيرا للأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading affirms both sons of Rachel stole according to appearances, using Joseph's alleged theft to disparage them; another treats both accusations as suspicions, with Benjamin's case reinforcing their old belief about Joseph.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل قولهم: إن يسرق فقد سرق أخ له من قبل تأويلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators supply ‘it was said about Joseph that he stole’; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says that gloss does not fit the verse's wording.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المفسرين: التقدير: فقد قيل عن يوسف إنه سرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers speak according to appearances and the applicable judgment, not as backbiters; they shift blame from themselves to the two full brothers.
rows.anchor: فلم يقعوا في غيبة ليوسف، وإنما قصدوا الإخبار بأمر جرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority story says Joseph's aunt hid Isaac's inherited belt beneath his clothes and accused him of taking it; their law let her keep him until she died.
rows.anchor: الجمهور منها على أن عمته كانت ربته، فلما شب أراد يعقوب أخذه منها

rows.speaker: ابن إدريس عن أبيه
rows.claim: Ibn Idrīs transmits from his father that Joseph hid a piece of meat at a meal and was accused of theft for taking it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إدريس عن أبيه: إنما أكل بنو يعقوب طعاما

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وقتادة
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Qatāda say Joseph's mother ordered him to steal and break her father's idol to correct wrongdoing; al-Zajjāj says it was gold.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير وقتادة: إنما أمرته أمه أن يسرق صنما لأبيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in fa-asarrah refers to the pain held in Jacob's soul, an unspoken antecedent supplied by context; the author compares this to al-Ḥāṭim's line and 16:110.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله: فأسرها عائد يراد به الحزة التي حدثت في نفس يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpreters say Joseph concealed retaliation or an argument; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the contextual sense. Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads fa-asarahu with a masculine pronoun.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: أسر المجازاة، وقال قوم: أسر الحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation has Joseph say openly that the brothers are worse in conduct; God's knowledge implicitly contradicts them, and their later plea appeals to their father rather than themselves.
rows.anchor: الظاهر منه أنه قالها إفصاحا فكأنه أسر لهم كراهية مقالتهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The apparent sense of Ibn ʿAbbās's view is that Joseph said nothing aloud; ‘you are worse’ explains the thought he kept to himself.
rows.anchor: وهو ظاهر كلام ابن عباس- لم يقل يوسف هذا الكلام إلا في نفسه

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī recounts that Benjamin blamed the brothers for selling Joseph and planting the cup; Joseph supposedly tapped it, which revealed the sale, and Benjamin asked it to tell the truth.
rows.anchor: وذكر الطبري هنا قصصا اختصاره: أنه لما استخرجت السقاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya abbreviates such extended tales rather than retelling them in full.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا من القصص الذي آثرنا اختصاره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A tale says Reuben's anger made his hair stand out, Joseph's son touched and calmed him, and the brothers considered fighting; Joseph then overpowered Reuben.
rows.anchor: وروي أن روبيل غضب ووقف شعره حتى خرج من ثيابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They call Joseph al-ʿAzīz because he holds that office after the former Aziz's reported death or dismissal.
rows.anchor: خاطبوه باسم العزيز إذ كان في تلك الخطة بعزل الأول أو موته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Take one of us in his place’ may be rhetorical pleading, since a free man cannot replace someone already enslaved; Joseph refuses to do what is unlawful.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون مجازا وهم يعلمون أنه لا يصح أخذ حر ليسترق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the brothers propose themselves as guarantors so Benjamin can return and explain matters; though they cannot plausibly seek another free man's enslavement, Joseph refuses because personal surety only ensures appearance and may be rejected.
rows.anchor: إلا أن يريدوا بذلك طريق الحمالة، أي خذ أحدنا حتى ينصرف إليك صاحبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surety that substitutes the guarantor for another person's punishment is unanimously unlawful; al-Wāḍiḥa allows personal surety in penalties except in a death case.
rows.anchor: فلا يجوز ذلك إجماعا. وفي الواضحة: إن الحمالة بالوجه فقط

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: ‘We see you as beneficent’ may describe Joseph's past generosity or, as Ibn Isḥāq says, ask him to show kindness now.
rows.anchor: وهذا تأويل ابن إسحاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿādh is a verbal noun taking no expressed verb; ẓulm here is literal wrongdoing, putting something where it does not belong.
rows.anchor: ومعاذ نصب على المصدر، ولا يجوز إظهار الفعل معه

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: A report cited by al-Ṭabarī says Joseph sent Jacob the king's greeting and prayer that he live until seeing Joseph, so he would know Egypt held two righteous men like him.
rows.anchor: وذكر الطبري أنه روي أن يوسف أيأسهم بلفظه هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istayʾas and istaʾyas both mean despair, like sakhira/istaskhara and ʿajiba/istaʿjaba; the author cites Qur'anic, poetic, and dialectal parallels.
rows.anchor: واستسخر، ومنه قوله تعالى: يستسخرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read istayʾasū; Ibn Kathīr has istaʾyasū and related forms in other verses. It derives by inversion from yāʾisa to āyisa, unlike jadaba/jabadha, which have separate roots.
rows.anchor: وهذه قراءة الجمهور، وقرأ ابن كثير: «استأيسوا» و «لا تأيسوا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalaṣū najiyyan means they withdrew to confer privately; najī can describe one or many, masculine or feminine, like ʿadu and ʿadl, and its plural is anjiya, as Labīd's verse shows.
rows.anchor: وقوله: خلصوا نجيا معناه انفردوا عن غيرهم يناجي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the eldest as Shimʿūn, best in judgment and knowledge though Reuben was older; Qatāda says Reuben by age, which Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabarī prefer as more apparent; al-Suddī says oldest in knowledge.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: هو شمعون لأنه كان كبيرهم رأيا وتدبيرا وعلما

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes ‘their eldest’ as Reuben, oldest by age; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this is more apparent, as does al-Ṭabarī.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هو روبيل لأنه أسنهم، وهذا أظهر ورجحه الطبري

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī understands the eldest as the most learned brother, who reminded them of Jacob's covenant.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: معنى الآية: وقال كبيرهم في العلم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī offers grammatical parses for mā in mā farraṭtum: extra, a subject, or an accusative coordinated with an understood ‘you know’; the author rejects connecting min qabl directly to the verb.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن يكون قوله: من قبل متعلقا ب فرطتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one parse mā is a verbal noun: ‘your neglect of Joseph before’; on another it is a relative or verbal noun in an accusative phrase coordinated with ‘you know.’
rows.anchor: التقدير: من قبل تفريطكم في يوسف واقع أو مستقر
